landing_meta_description: {name} is a free, open-source surf forecast app. Live swell, wind and tide, plus a 7-day forecast, all on one map. Save your spots, get alerted when they're working, and log every session.
landing_hero_title: The surf forecast that {word} you when your spot is working.

landing_hero_push_2_text: Until noon: 2.1 m at 12 s from the west-northwest, 8 kn offshore.
landing_hero_push_3_text: 8 to 11 am: 1.5 m at 10 s from the southwest, tide dropping.
landing_hero_push_4_title: Hossegor picks up in an hour
landing_hero_push_4_text: 5 to 8 pm: 1.6 m at 13 s from the west, 4 kn offshore.
landing_hero_body: Live swell, wind and tide, plus the next 7 days, all on one map.
landing_hero_free: Free · Open source · No account needed for the map

landing_sources_title: {live} buoys and wind, straight from the source.
landing_sources_more: {name} reads the public buoy and wind-station networks, plus open forecast models. Every one is credited, licence included.
sources_page_more: Who measured the sea {name} shows, how often it is read, and on what terms.
sources_named_text: Every figure says its source and its licence, in the app and in the API.
sources_open_text: Only sources whose terms allow it, read where they publish.
sources_kept_text: No data is taken from another app or another site.
sources_candhis_text: The national network of wave buoys along the French coasts, kept by Cerema with its partners.
sources_copernicus_in_situ_text: The buoys of the national institutes, Spain's and Ireland's among them, gathered by the European marine service.
sources_ndbc_text: The American network of buoys and coastal stations, which also relays its partners' around the world. Waves and wind.
sources_irish_lights_text: The buoys and weather stations of the Irish lighthouse service. Waves and wind.
sources_marine_institute_text: The weather buoys far off the Irish coast, M2 to M6. Waves and wind.
sources_hidrografico_text: The wave buoys of the Portuguese Navy's hydrographic institute.
sources_fmi_text: The wave buoys of the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
sources_queensland_text: The wave buoys of the Queensland Government, along its coast.
sources_meteo_france_text: The ground stations of the French weather service: wind and gusts.
sources_openwindmap_text: A community network of wind beacons, Pioupiou among them, often set right on the spots.
sources_dmi_text: The stations of the Danish weather service, many on lighthouses and harbours: wind and gusts.
sources_rijkswaterstaat_text: The stations of the Dutch authority of the coast: on the shore, on the Wadden and on the platforms of the North Sea.
sources_jma_text: AMeDAS, the automatic stations of the Japanese weather service, many on capes and harbours.
sources_coops_text: The weather sensors of NOAA's tide stations, on piers and harbours, on the shore itself: wind and gusts.
sources_ipma_text: The stations of the Portuguese weather institute, every hour.
sources_aemet_text: The automatic stations of the Spanish weather agency, with gusts, on an instance that holds a key.
sources_metar_text: The reports of the world's airports, where no other station stands near: wind and gusts.
sources_open_meteo_text: Wind and weather at any point from the models of DWD, Météo-France and NOAA, at 2 to 13 km, and the waves and the swell apart from Météo-France's model, at 8 km: read from the open files behind Open-Meteo's API, which answers itself when a file cannot be read.
sources_copernicus_models_text: The Met Office's fine model, at 1.5 km from the Vendée to Norway, and the map of wave heights.
sources_neaps_text: Tides computed from open harmonic constants, at the nearest port. They are not SHOM's predictions, so there is no coefficient yet.
sources_catalogue_text: The breaks the instance's operator added, completed by what accounts write of them. A spot an account makes public joins it under the ODbL.
sources_openfreemap_text: The map under everything, drawn from OpenStreetMap.
sources_natural_earth_text: The coastline that tells a wind station of the coast from one inland, so that a wide view shows the sea's wind first.
sources_photon_text: Finding a place by its name, for an account.
sources_missing_text: Tell me which one, and where it publishes. The technical detail of every source, its access and its terms, is in the repository.

landing_story_me: I finally brought surfing and code together.
landing_story_origin_after: , made by Thomas. It made me want to build my own, with the things I was missing: spots, the conditions that make them work, alerts, and plenty more. Thanks, Thomas.
landing_story_feedback: I'm building it on my own, and the app is still young. If something feels off, drop me a line: every message counts.
landing_next_more: None of this is promised yet: tell me which one you want most.
landing_next_mobile_text: iOS and Android, with alerts as push notifications.
landing_next_data_text: New buoy networks, and a much bigger catalogue of spots.

terms_guide_title: What you write in a guide
terms_guide_text: What you write of a public spot is read by everyone, under your username, once a moderator or the people who keep the spot confirmed it. A list of words joins the catalogue of {name} under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0, and a text under the Database Contents License (DbCL) 1.0.
terms_guide_rights: By sending, you confirm that you wrote it yourself, from what you know of the place, and you accept these licences. What you wrote stays when your account is deleted, and then names nobody.
terms_reports_title: What you show in a report
terms_reports_text: A report shows the photos and videos you send of a public spot to everyone, under your username, for a week. They are checked first: shot at the spot, in the two hours before you sent them, and showing the waves. One that does not pass is shown to no one, and any account may flag one it thinks should not be shown. A moderator may hide or remove a report.
terms_reports_rights: By sending, you confirm that you shot them yourself, and that no one can be recognised close up in them without their agreement. You keep your rights over them, and you let {publisher} keep them, make them smaller and show them on {name}, its pages and its API, for as long as the report is kept. Delete the report, or your account, and they go.

privacy_meta_description: What {name} keeps of its visitors and its accounts, why, for how long, and who receives it.
privacy_who_text: This page says what {name} keeps about you, why, who else receives it, and how to have it corrected or deleted. {publisher} runs this instance and is responsible for this data. Write to this address about any of it:
privacy_visit_text: Reading the map takes no account. Cloudflare serves the web app, so it receives your IP address and the pages you open, as any host does. To draw the map, your browser loads its tiles from OpenFreeMap and the colours of the sea from Copernicus Marine: both see your IP address and the part of the map you look at.
privacy_visit_browser: Your browser keeps your settings for the app: your language in a cookie, and in its own storage the map's last position, its layers, your units, your shortcuts and the places you looked at last. Without an account they stay there, and none of them tracks you.
privacy_visit_audience: Umami, which {publisher} runs, counts the pages read here, the landing's too: the page, the site you came from, your browser, your system, the kind and size of your screen, your language and your country. It sets no cookie and keeps neither your IP address nor the page's query, and it tells two visits of one browser apart by a code that changes every month.
privacy_account_text: An account keeps your email address, your username, which others can read, and your password, stored hashed and never in clear. A cookie keeps your session open, for up to 90 days after you last used the app. At sign-up, a mail with a link checks your address, and the link works for a day. If you forget your password, a mail with a link lets you choose another: the link works once, for an hour, and choosing signs your account out everywhere. If you sign in with Google, Google gives us your name, your email address and your profile picture, and the tokens of that sign-in are kept with your account. Google tells us nothing else. If you sign in with Apple, Apple gives us your name, the first time only, and your email address, or, if you chose to hide it, an address of Apple's that passes our mails on to you. The tokens of that sign-in are kept with your account.
privacy_account_sessions: Each sign-in is kept with the IP address and the browser it came from, for the security of your account. Nothing in the app shows them, and they are kept as long as the account exists.
privacy_content_text: The app keeps what you make in it: your spots and lists, your alerts and what they told you, your log of sessions with its notes and what the sea did, what you said of your surfing (your level, the waves you surf, how you read a forecast and your boards), the places you looked at last, your units and your shortcuts. Your spots, your sessions and what you said of your surfing are yours alone. Others read something of yours only in these cases:
privacy_content_shared: A list you share by a link is read by whoever has the link, with the private spots in it.
privacy_content_public: A spot you ask to make public is read by the operator who decides. Once accepted, it joins the catalogue without your name.
privacy_content_guides: What you write in a guide is read by everyone, under your username, once it is confirmed.
privacy_content_reports: A report you send at a public spot is read by everyone, under your username, for a week, with how far from the spot its photos were taken.
privacy_content_sizes: How big the waves looked in your sessions at a spot of the catalogue counts, with everyone else's, toward one figure shown to whoever opens that spot: how its waves run against the forecast, with the number of sessions it comes from. Neither your name nor your session is shown.
privacy_content_friends: Your friends read your username, your rank and your confirmed contributions.
privacy_content_operator: The operator of the instance reads each account's email address and username, whether the address is checked and whether the account is suspended. {publisher} runs the server and can read the database, but reads it only to keep the service running or to answer a request.
privacy_content_media: The photos and videos you add to a session are kept by Cloudflare, in its R2 storage, once made smaller. What a file said about where, when and with what it was taken is removed, and the file you sent is deleted once made. You alone see them, through links that work for two hours at most, and they go with their session or your account within minutes.
privacy_reports: When you send a report, we read where and when its photos and videos were taken from the files, or, when a file does not say, where your phone stands as you send, if you let the browser tell us. That position is kept only when it is within two kilometres of the spot. Two models running on our own server check that the photos show the waves and no nudity: nothing is sent elsewhere. The files are made smaller and lose what they said of where, when and with what they were shot. A report stops being shown after a week, and is kept, as are the flags of other accounts, until you delete it or your account.
privacy_alerts_mail: Unosend sends the mail that checks your address, the one that lets you choose a new password and, if you choose alerts by mail, the mails of your alerts. It receives your address, the names of the alert and of its spots, and what the alert found. You may leave the names out of the subject. Each alert mail has a link that stops them, and no mail carries a tracker.
privacy_alerts_push: If you turn on push in a browser, we keep the address its push service gave it, its keys and the name of the browser. Each push goes through that service, run by Google, Mozilla, Apple or Microsoft depending on your browser, encrypted so that the service cannot read it. A browser is forgotten when you sign out of it or remove it. A push about a report carries the address of its first photo, which works for a few hours.
privacy_search_text: When you search for a place by its name, our server asks Photon, a service of komoot, in Germany. It sends what you typed, your language and the centre of the map, rounded to about ten kilometres, and nothing about your account. The search is neither kept nor logged.
privacy_agents_text: If you sign an AI assistant in to your account, we keep its registration, your agreement and its tokens. It can then read your spots, your alerts, what they told you, your sessions and what you said of your surfing, and change nothing. Its access lasts an hour and renews itself for up to 30 days after it was last used. You disconnect it from your account's panel. What the assistant does with what it read is up to whoever provides it.
privacy_analytics_more: PostHog keeps these events and reports in its European cloud. They reach it through the app's own address, without your IP address, and PostHog is told not to locate you. Your choice is kept in your browser for six months, then asked again. The landing page sends PostHog nothing.
privacy_contact_text: The forms of this site that write to {publisher} send your first name, your address and your message by mail to {email}. Nothing of them is kept in the database: the mail is all there is.
privacy_running_text: The API counts its calls by hour, by kind of caller and by outcome, never by account. What you ask of the forecasts is counted apart, by the hour, to your account, or to a hash of your IP address when you have none, so that one caller cannot spend the day's forecasts of everyone: these counts are kept two days. Its log notes each request's method, path and status, without your IP address. What an operator does, such as suspending an account, is recorded with that account's identifier. The database is backed up by its host. When the API itself fails, it sends PostHog a report of the fault: what failed and where in its code, with nothing of the request, the account or the person who made it.
privacy_bases_contract: Your account, what you save, mails and push, place search and assistants: providing the service you asked for (GDPR, article 6(1)(b)).
privacy_bases_consent: Usage analytics and the app's error reports: your consent (article 6(1)(a)), which you withdraw at any time in the account's panel.
privacy_bases_interest: Audience counts, sign-in records, call counts, the log, the API's fault reports, backups and moderation: our legitimate interest in keeping the service secure and running (article 6(1)(f)).
privacy_bases_messages: Messages you send us: our legitimate interest in answering them (article 6(1)(f)).

learn_beginner_title: How to read a surf forecast: the basics
learn_beginner_lead: A forecast comes down to five figures: the height of the waves, their [period](period), where the [swell](swell) comes from, the wind and the [tide](tide). Five lessons, one demo each. Ten minutes before your first session.
learn_beginner_meta_title: How to read a surf forecast: height, period, swell, wind and tide
learn_beginner_meta_description: The basics of a surf forecast before a first session: the height announced, the period, the swell's direction and a spot's window, offshore and onshore wind, the tide. With demos you move yourself.
learn_intermediate_title: Reading a week of forecasts and finding the right window
learn_intermediate_lead: You surf already and want to pick your day. [Swell](swell) and [wind sea](wind-sea), [energy](energy), [fetch](fetch), a week read at a glance, and why two spots a few kilometres apart do not work on the same day.

learn_advanced_lead: What the figures are made of: the [models](model) and their [resolution](resolution), the gap between a [buoy](buoy) and a model, swells that overlap, the [shadow](shadowing) of an island, and an alert drawn from your sessions.

learn_b_height_p1: The height announced is that of the [swell](swell) **out at sea**: trough to crest, measured by a [buoy](buoy) or computed by a [model](model). It is not the height of the wave you will see at the beach.
learn_b_height_p2: At the shore, the wave stands up as it touches the bottom, and it is often **taller than the swell announced**: {one} out at sea can give {more} on a [reef](reef), and less on a beach that spreads it out. The gap depends on the period and the bottom.
learn_b_height_p3: To start, look for a swell forecast at **{from} to {to}**. Above {above}, you spend the session paddling.
learn_b_height_keep: The color of the sea on the map is that height.
learn_b_height_hint: Slide. The color is the one this sea has on the map, and the surfer beside the wave is {surfer} tall.
learn_b_period_p1: The [period](period) is the **time between two waves**, in seconds. It is the figure beginners skip, and the one that says the most.
learn_b_period_p2: A **14 s** swell has crossed the ocean: long, orderly, powerful, it grows as it reaches the shore. An **8 s** swell was born close by, in the wind: short, messy, it breaks any old way. At the same height, a 14 s wave carries three times the [energy](energy) of an 8 s one, and looks bigger.
learn_b_period_p3: Under 8 s, it is [chop](chop). From 8 to 11 s, it can be surfed. From 12 s up, it is a real swell: exposed spots get big, sheltered spots wake up.
learn_b_period_keep: At the same height, look at the period first.
learn_b_period_hint: Same height. Slide from 8 to 14 s: the waves spread out, and the energy triples.
learn_b_swell_p1: The direction is **where the swell comes from**, as for the wind: a west swell comes from the west. {name} writes it with an arrow that points the way it goes, then the name of the point it comes from.
learn_b_swell_p2: A spot only receives the swell that enters its [window](window): the part of the horizon it sees from the beach. A beach that faces west takes swells from the south-west to the north-west. A north swell passes offshore and leaves the beach flat, while the buoy says {height}.
learn_b_swell_p3: On a spot's page, the window is drawn as a ring. When the sea's sentence judges "the swell's direction", it says whether today's swell enters that window.
learn_b_swell_keep: {height} at the buoy does nothing for a spot that cannot see it.
learn_b_swell_hint: Change the swell's direction in front of a beach that faces west. The ring is its window, as on a spot's page.
learn_b_wind_p1: The wind is named **from the beach**. [Offshore](offshore): it comes from the land and blows out to sea. It smooths the wave, holds it up, hollows it. [Onshore](onshore): it comes from the sea. It makes the wave break too early, soft and messy. [Cross-shore](side-shore): it runs along the beach, and gets in the way without ruining everything.
learn_b_wind_p2: The same wind is offshore here and onshore on the next beach, which faces another way. That is why {name} names it **spot by spot**.
learn_b_wind_p3: Strength counts as much: up to {calm}, almost anything goes. Beyond {strong}, even offshore, it holds you at the top of the wave on the [take-off](take-off).
learn_b_wind_keep: At dawn, there is often little wind. That is why sessions happen early.
learn_b_wind_hint: Change the wind's direction in front of the same beach, then its strength: the wave smooths out or gets chopped up.
learn_b_tide_p1: The [tide](tide) changes the **depth of water over the bottom**, and so how the wave breaks. At [low tide](low-water), the bottom is close: the wave breaks fast, hollow, sometimes too much. At [high tide](high-water), there is too much water: it breaks softly, or not at all. At [mid-tide](mid-tide), in between, most beaches work.
learn_b_tide_p2: Every spot has **its own tide**. Some only work at low tide, others only wake up at high tide. A spot's page says so when it is known, and the sea's sentence tells you whether the tide right now suits it.
learn_b_tide_p3: [Rising](rising) or [falling](falling) counts too: the rising tide pushes the swell towards the beach and often makes things better; the falling tide empties the spot.
learn_b_tide_keep: Look at the time of [high water](high-water) before you look at the height.
learn_b_tide_hint: Run through the day: the water rises and falls over the bottom of the spot.
learn_g_swell_what: Waves that have left the wind that raised them and travel on their own, regular, over hundreds or thousands of kilometres.
learn_g_swell_from: A storm blows for days over a stretch of ocean, the [fetch](fetch), and raises a choppy sea there. As they travel away, the waves sort themselves by speed, the longest in front. Your beach gets waves that are already sorted, clean and regular. The further and stronger the storm, the longer the [period](period).
learn_g_wind_sea_what: The waves raised by the wind blowing right now, where you are: short, messy, of brief period.
learn_g_wind_sea_from: The wind pushes the surface of the water and wrinkles it. As long as it blows, the waves stay under it, choppy. Once it drops or they move away, they become a [swell](swell).
learn_g_period_what: The time between two crests, in seconds. It is the speed and the energy of the swell in one figure: a 14 s swell moves at over 40 km/h in deep water and feels the bottom much sooner than an 8 s one.
learn_g_period_from: From the distance travelled. Near the storm, every period mixes; far from it, only the long ones have arrived, because they travel faster.
learn_g_set_what: A group of bigger waves that arrives after several minutes of calm, then goes. Surfers wait for them in the [lineup](lineup).
learn_g_set_from: Two swells of close periods overlap: when their crests coincide, the waves add up; when they oppose, they cancel out. Sets are that beat.
learn_g_chop_what: Small, short, messy waves raised by the wind of the moment, under 8 s of period. It cannot be surfed, or only badly.
learn_g_chop_from: From local wind, which has blown neither long nor far: the waves had no time to grow or to sort themselves.
learn_g_buoy_what: A float anchored out at sea, which measures the waves that lift it and sends its readings every half hour. It is the real sea, not a forecast.
learn_g_buoy_from: From the measuring networks of states and institutes. The sources page names every buoy {name} reads, with its licence.
learn_g_model_what: A program that computes tomorrow's sea from the forecast wind, on a grid of a few kilometres, several times a day. A forecast is the result of a model.
learn_g_model_from: Weather services solve the equations of water and air for the whole planet. Each computation, or [run](run), starts again from the latest measurements.
learn_g_window_what: The part of the horizon a spot sees from its beach: only the swells that come from it reach the spot. On a spot's page, a ring draws it.
learn_g_window_from: From the shape of the coast. A headland, an island or a bay hide a part of the horizon, and the swell that comes from there passes offshore or arrives weakened.
learn_g_sector_what: The direction a swell or a wind comes from, said as a point of the compass: a west swell comes from the west. {name} writes it with an arrow that points the way it goes, then the name of the point.
learn_g_sector_from: From navigation, which has always named winds by their origin. Surfing kept the habit.
learn_g_offshore_what: A wind that comes from the land and blows out to sea. It holds up the lip of the wave, which stands taller and hollower before breaking. It is the wind everyone hopes for.
learn_g_offshore_from: Often from the night. The land cools faster than the sea, and the cool air flows from the land out to sea. It is the land breeze of dawn, which drops once the sun warms up.
learn_g_onshore_what: A wind that comes from the sea. It pushes the wave in the back, flattens it, and makes it break too early, soft and messy.
learn_g_onshore_from: Often from the afternoon. The sun warms the land, the air rises there, and air from the sea comes to take its place. It is the sea breeze, which picks up around noon in fine weather.
learn_g_side_shore_what: A wind that runs along the beach. It gets in the wave's way without ruining everything, and pushes the surfer along the shore. In between, {name} says cross-offshore and cross-onshore.
learn_g_side_shore_from: From the angle between the wind and the coast: the same wind is cross-shore here and [offshore](offshore) on the next beach, which faces another way.
learn_g_knot_what: The unit of speed of the sea and the air: one nautical mile an hour, 1.85 km/h. Ten knots is a breeze; twenty-five, a wind that ruins the session.
learn_g_knot_from: From sailors, who measured the speed of the ship by counting the knots of a rope paid out behind it. {name} writes the wind in the unit you choose.
learn_g_tide_what: The rise and fall of the sea, twice a day. It changes the depth of water over the bottom, and so the wave.
learn_g_tide_from: From the Moon and the Sun, which pull the water of the oceans. The Earth turns under that bulge: the sea rises and falls about every six hours, a little later each day.
learn_g_high_water_what: The moment the sea is at its highest, before it falls again. The app writes it "high water", with its time.
learn_g_high_water_from: The bulge of water the Moon pulls passes your coast. On many spots there is then too much water over the bottom, and the wave breaks softly.
learn_g_low_water_what: The moment the sea is at its lowest, before it rises again. The app writes it "low water", with its time.
learn_g_low_water_from: The sea is between two bulges. The bottom is close: the wave breaks fast and hollow, sometimes too much, and rocks come out of the water.
learn_g_mid_tide_what: Halfway between low and high tide, when the water rises or falls fastest. It is the moment of most beaches.
learn_g_mid_tide_from: From the shape of the tide, which moves faster in the middle of its course than at either end: the sailors' rule of twelfths.
learn_g_rising_what: When the sea rises, from low tide towards high tide. It pushes the swell towards the beach, and often makes things better.
learn_g_rising_from: The bulge is coming. The current that flows towards the land helps the wave stand up.
learn_g_falling_what: When the sea falls, from high tide towards low tide. It empties the spot, and the current flowing back out to sea can flatten the wave.
learn_g_falling_from: The bulge is leaving. The current that flows out to sea works against the wave coming in.
learn_g_spring_tides_what: The days when the tide rises highest and falls lowest, every fortnight. In France, the coefficient says them in one figure: 95 and above.
learn_g_spring_tides_from: From the Moon and the Sun lined up, at new and full moon, pulling the same way. At first and last quarter they pull at right angles: those are the neap tides, and the tide barely moves.
learn_g_reef_what: A bottom of rock or coral. The wave always breaks in the same place there, often hollower than on sand, and the bottom does not forgive.
learn_g_reef_from: A bank of rocks or a shelf the swell meets all at once: it stands up fast, hence its shape. Many famous spots are reefs.
learn_g_beach_break_what: A wave that breaks on sand. The banks move with the storms and the tides: the peak changes place from one week to the next. It is where people learn.
learn_g_beach_break_from: From sand that the currents lay down in banks. The swell breaks on the bank, then the wave rolls to the shore.
learn_g_point_break_what: A wave that breaks along a headland or a cape and peels in one direction, sometimes for a very long way.
learn_g_point_break_from: From a swell that arrives at an angle on a coast that juts out: it wraps around the point by [refraction](refraction) and breaks bit by bit.
learn_g_take_off_what: The moment you stand up on the board, at the top of the wave as it rises. The wind, the tide and the bottom decide whether it is easy.
learn_g_take_off_from: From English, like most of surfing's words.
learn_g_fetch_what: The stretch of ocean over which a wind blows in the same direction. The longer it is and the longer the wind lasts, the bigger and longer the swell.
learn_g_fetch_from: From the winter storms of the North Atlantic and the Pacific, which blow for days over thousands of kilometres: that is where the great swells come from.
learn_g_energy_what: What a wave carries, in one figure that combines its height and its period. The week's table writes it in kilojoules per metre of crest. At the same height, two waves of different periods do not carry the same energy.
learn_g_energy_from: From physics: the energy of a wave grows with the square of its height and the square of its period. Double the period, and you quadruple the energy.
learn_g_resolution_what: The size of the cells of the grid a model computes on: 25 km for a global model, 8 km for the wave model {name} reads, 2 km for a coastal one. A cell sees nothing smaller than itself.
learn_g_resolution_from: From the cost of computing: cells half as big mean eight times the computation. Fine models cover one region only.
learn_g_run_what: One computation of the model, started several times a day from the latest measurements. The forecast changes from one run to the next: that is normal.
learn_g_run_from: From the fixed hours of the weather services, often 0, 6, 12 and 18 universal time. {name} says when it read its forecast.
learn_g_secondary_swell_what: A second swell, from another direction or of another period, that arrives at the same time as the main one. The week's table shows it apart.
learn_g_secondary_swell_from: From two storms at once, or one storm that has turned. The two swells cross, and the [sets](set) come from their beat.
learn_g_shadowing_what: The part of the sea an island, a cape or a peninsula hides from a swell: behind them, it arrives weakened or not at all.
learn_g_shadowing_from: A swell goes straight. What lies in its path receives it; what is hidden behind an obstacle only gets what [refraction](refraction) brings back.
learn_g_refraction_what: The swell bending as it nears a coast: it slows where the bottom rises, and turns to arrive square to the beach, or to wrap around a point.
learn_g_refraction_from: From the speed of the wave, which depends on the depth near the shore. The side that touches the bottom first slows down, and the wave pivots, like a car braking on one side.
learn_g_exposure_what: How much swell a spot receives, depending on whether it faces the open sea or is sheltered. An exposed spot gets big as soon as a swell rises; a sheltered one waits for a big swell.
learn_g_exposure_from: From the shape of the coast and the bottom, which filter the swell. Two spots a few kilometres apart do not have the same exposure.
learn_g_significant_height_what: The height buoys and models announce: the mean of the highest third of the waves. One wave in ten is above it, one in a thousand is almost twice it.
learn_g_significant_height_from: From oceanographers, who found that this figure matches what a sailor estimates by eye. The biggest waves of a [set](set) are above it.
learn_g_lineup_what: The place, out from the shore, where surfers wait for the waves, where they start to break.
learn_g_lineup_from: From the surfers lined up facing the open sea.
learn_intermediate_meta_title: Reading a week of surf forecasts: swell, wind sea, energy, fetch
learn_intermediate_meta_description: To pick your day: swell and wind sea read apart, the energy of a wave, the fetch of a storm, a week read at a glance, and why two neighbouring spots do not work on the same day.
learn_advanced_meta_title: Wave models, buoys and secondary swells: understanding a surf forecast
learn_advanced_meta_description: What the figures of a surf forecast are made of: the resolution of the models, the gap between a buoy and a model, secondary swells, shadow and refraction, and an alert drawn from your sessions.
learn_i_windsea_p1: The week's table shows two things in the waves: the [swell](swell), which comes from afar, and the [wind sea](wind-sea), raised by the day's wind. The total height combines the two without adding them up, and it is what many sites announce.
learn_i_windsea_p2: The two are not worth the same. {name} shows them apart: the swell alone says what there will be to surf, and the wind sea says whether it will be clean. {total} announced can be {swell} of swell under a strong wind sea.
learn_i_windsea_p3: Look at the swell's line first, then its [period](period). Then ask what the wind adds: if it is light or [offshore](offshore), nothing; if it has blown from the sea for hours, a wind sea that chops everything up.
learn_i_windsea_keep: Do not trust the total height: read the swell's line.
learn_i_windsea_hint: The swell stays at {height} and {period}. Raise the local wind: the wind sea adds up, and the total grows without the session getting any better.
learn_i_energy_p1: Height and [period](period) are read together, and one figure holds them: the [energy](energy), which the week's table writes in kilojoules per metre of crest. It grows with the square of one and the square of the other.
learn_i_energy_p2: {low} at {lowPeriod} carries as much energy as {high} at {highPeriod}. The first is a clean swell that will stand up at the shore; the second, a short sea that crumbles. At equal energy, the long period always wins.
learn_i_energy_p3: On a spot you know, note the energy of the days you liked. It is often a better marker than the height alone, because it counts the period too.
learn_i_energy_keep: Two figures in one: at equal energy, take the longer period.
learn_i_energy_hint: {low} at {lowPeriod} and {high} at {highPeriod} both make {energy}. Slide both: the period weighs as much as the height.
learn_i_fetch_p1: A swell is born of a wind that blows long, hard, in the same direction, over a wide stretch of ocean: the [fetch](fetch). The longer the fetch and the stronger the wind, the bigger the swell, and the longer its period.
learn_i_fetch_p2: Once on its way, the swell travels alone, and the long periods go faster: a {period} swell covers nearly {distance} a day. That is why a storm on the other side of the Atlantic announces itself four or five days ahead, and a low passing near the coast raises a short sea without warning.
learn_i_fetch_p3: On the map, a red patch out at sea is a storm. The color that moves towards the coast over the following days is its swell arriving, the long periods first.
learn_i_fetch_keep: A long period is a distant storm: you can see it coming days ahead.
learn_i_fetch_hint: The beach is {distance} away. Strengthen the wind and lengthen the fetch: the swell grows, its period lengthens, and it arrives sooner.
learn_i_week_p1: A week is read at a glance: first the [swell](swell) and its [period](period), day by day, to see when it comes in; then the wind, hour by hour, to see when it stays clean; then the [tide](tide), to pick the hour.
learn_i_week_p2: The right window is when the three cross: enough swell, a period that holds, and a wind under {wind} or [offshore](offshore). It often lasts three hours, not a day: the morning before the breeze picks up, or the evening when it drops.
learn_i_week_p3: That is what a {name} alert watches for you: you say what your spot likes, it reads the week and tells you the evening before.
learn_i_week_keep: Look for the hour, not the day.
learn_i_week_hint: Run through the three days: the hours that work are marked under the bars. Look for when the swell is there and the wind is still asleep.
learn_i_neighbours_p1: Two spots {distance} apart do not always work on the same day, and that is normal. Each has its [window](window), its [exposure](exposure), its bottom and its tide.
learn_i_neighbours_p2: A beach that faces west takes everything that comes from the Atlantic and saturates fast. A cove that faces south, behind a headland, only receives the swells that turn, by [refraction](refraction), and stays surfable when the beach is closed out. The same wind is [cross-shore](side-shore) at one and [offshore](offshore) at the other.
learn_i_neighbours_p3: That is the game: when the exposed one closes out, the sheltered one lights up. Each spot's page says what it likes; compare them before you load the car.
learn_i_neighbours_keep: When your spot closes out, its sheltered neighbour may be opening.
learn_i_neighbours_hint: Turn the swell: each spot has its ring. A north-west swell lights up the beach; a south-west swell wakes the cove.
learn_a_models_p1: A forecast comes out of a [model](model), a program that computes the ocean on a grid. {name} reads the waves from a model with an 8 km grid, and the wind from models of 2 to 13 km depending on the region. A cell sees nothing smaller than itself. For a model at 25 km, a three-kilometre cove does not exist.
learn_a_models_p2: The model computes out at sea, in deep water. The figure of a coastal cell is the swell that arrives. The wave that breaks depends on the bottom, the headland and the bay, which are too small for its [resolution](resolution).
learn_a_models_p3: Each [run](run) starts again from the latest measurements and corrects the previous one. The forecast therefore changes every day, and the far days change the most. A spot's page says at what time its forecast was read.
learn_a_models_keep: A figure holds for its cell, out at sea, at the hour of its run.
learn_a_models_seen: The cove has its own cell
learn_a_models_unseen: The cove does not exist for the model
learn_a_models_hint: Change the resolution. At 25 km, the cove is lost in a cell of land. At 2 km, it has a cell of its own.
learn_a_buoys_p1: A [buoy](buoy) measures, a model computes. The buoy gives the sea of half an hour ago, with its [sets](set) and its mess. The model gives a smoothed sea, for now and the seven days ahead.
learn_a_buoys_p2: The two always differ a little, often by {gap} in height. The further ahead you look, the wider the gap. At two days, the model is reliable. At four, it gives the trend. At seven, it guesses. When the buoy and the model disagree about the same hour, trust the buoy.
learn_a_buoys_p3: On the map, {name} shows the two curves together: the buoy's up to now, and the model's, which goes on after it. Look at today's gap. If it is wide, trust the rest of the week less.
learn_a_buoys_keep: The buoy says what is happening. The model says what is coming, and errs more the further ahead it looks.
learn_a_buoys_hint: Move through the week, and the cone widens. The solid line is the buoy, the dashed line the model.
learn_a_secondary_p1: There is rarely one swell alone. A [secondary swell](secondary-swell), from another storm or another direction, lies over the main one. The week's table writes the main swell under the height of the waves. When the waves are much higher than the swell, other swells or the [wind sea](wind-sea) add to it.
learn_a_secondary_p2: When two swells cross, they make [sets](set). Where their crests meet, the waves add up. In between, the sea calms down. A short secondary swell, raised by the local wind, chops up the main one. A long one from another direction gives peaks that shift.
learn_a_secondary_p3: Read the main swell for the size, and the secondary one for the shape. A spot whose window opens to only one of the two gets only that one.
learn_a_secondary_keep: The main swell makes the size, the secondary one makes the shape.
learn_a_secondary_hint: Raise the second swell. The two trains cross, and once it is bigger than the other, it becomes the main one.
learn_a_shadow_p1: A swell goes straight. An island, a cape or a peninsula casts a [shadow](shadowing) on it. Behind them, it arrives weakened, or not at all. That is why a whole coast can stay flat with two metres out at sea.
learn_a_shadow_p2: [Refraction](refraction) shrinks the shadow. Near the shore, the swell slows where the bottom rises, and bends. It gets around a headland, enters a bay, and arrives square to a beach it was reaching from the side. It is what makes [point breaks](point-break) peel.
learn_a_shadow_p3: Under the same swell, one spot can be in the shadow and its neighbour exposed, a few degrees apart. When something stands between the open sea and you, the exact direction counts more than the height.
learn_a_shadow_keep: Behind an island, a few degrees of direction make all the difference.
learn_a_shadow_hint: Turn the swell around the island. The spot enters its shadow, then leaves it. Further behind the island, the shadow narrows and fades, because refraction brings the swell back in.
learn_a_alert_p1: All of this is for knowing which conditions you like at your spot, and being told when they come back. {name} keeps a log of your sessions: where, when, and the rating you give them. It adds what the sea was doing, even for a session written afterwards.
learn_a_alert_p2: From your best-rated sessions, it draws the conditions you like at a spot: the height, the period, the wind, in the words of an alert. It waits until it has at least three. The more sessions you rate, the surer those conditions are.
learn_a_alert_p3: An alert made of those figures watches the week for you and tells you the evening before. That is the end of the course. You no longer have to read the forecast every day, the alert does it for you.
learn_a_alert_keep: The more sessions you rate, the closer your alert gets to what you like.
learn_a_alert_none: It takes at least {count} sessions above the bar to draw an alert from them.
learn_a_alert_hint: Raise the lowest rating. Only the best sessions remain, and the alert narrows to them.
